newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: KNP BT seen posting sharp Q3 profit fall.
newsitem.headline: KNP BT seen posting sharp Q3 profit fall.

text.p: Paper, office supplies and printing equipment group NV Koninklijke KNP BT is expected to report a sharp profit fall for the 1996 third quarter on Thursday, financial analysts said.

Forecasts for the company's third quarter net, before a fixed dividend paid to preference shareholders, ranged from 33 to 45 million guilders, with an average of 39 million. In the 1995 third quarter, KNP BT posted a 116 million guilder profit.
In July, it said this year's second half would be better than the first, when profits fell by 64 percent, but warned that the traditionally weak third quarter would show another drop.
"I assume they will be able to earn a bit more in the second half of 1996 than in the first half, but the third quarter will be pretty weak," analyst Ad van de Laar at Bank Labouchere said.

"They earned 101 million guilders in the first half of the year and I expect that to rise to 119 million in the second half, with the accent on the fourth quarter," he added. For the third quarter he expects a net of about 35 million guilders.
Robert-Jan Stassen of Bank Bangert Pontier, predicting a third quarter net of only 33 million, pointed out that KNP BT's fourth quarter is traditionally its best period.
A recovery from the weak first half of 1996 would therefore be realised in the final quarter, rather than in the third.

Jan Wirken at research institute IRIS was slightly more optimistic with a third quarter profit forecast of 39 million guilders but he added that this figure could turn out lower if the company decided to take extraordinary charges.
KNP BT, which posted a 1995 full-year net from ordinary operations of 545 million guilders, has predicted that poor paper markets will depress its results this year.
Analysts said that given the prevailing overcapacity, price rises announced by KNP BT are proving difficult to implement.
"The price rises which KNP BT had in mind turned out to be rather a disappointment," Wirken said. He said the overcapacity among producers was not expected to abate before 1998.
Labouchere's Van de Laar said that KNP BT might not be able to raise selling prices to the same extent that raw materials prices had risen because of the difficult market.
"Even if you raise your (selling) prices you can still be squeezed," Labouchere's Van de Laar said.
Stassen of Bangert Pontier said the entire paper industry had originally attributed last year's booming sales to sound economic growth and above average levels of paper consumption.
"But it then proved to be a sort of advance-buying by clients, who were building up enormous supplies," he added.
However, most analysts expect paper markets will have bottomed out by the end of this year because paper users have already begun to cut their supplies.

All of them interepret KNP BT's decision to seek a partner for its 72-percent owned paper division KNP Leykam as a signal that it might eventually withdraw completely from the paper business, the most cyclical of its businesses.
"I think an underlying factor is that KNP BT wants to slowly withdraw from the paper market," Bangert Pontier's Stassen said.
Van de Laar said KNP BT's aim was to create greater added value for its shareholders, for which the only solution was spinning off the most cyclical part of the company.

Wirken said he thought KNP BT would be willing to sell its paper division if they could get a good price but added that major decisions on KNP Leykam could be up to two years away. By that time the unit would have new and more efficient production capacity and the market would probably have recovered, he said.
-- Theo Kolker, Amsterdam newsroom +31 20 504 5000
